primary_topics: Guest of Honor address at the program marking the 113th Anniversary of the Historic Siege of Baler and the 10th Philippine-Spanish Friendship Day, June 30, 2012 -- invited by Senator Edgardo J. Angara

The Siege of Baler: 50 Spanish cazadores under Capitan Enrique de las Morenas holding out for 337 days in the parish church; surrender June 2, 1899; President Aguinaldo's decree of June 30, 1899 declaring them 'not prisoners but friends'
Three milestones: (1) 113th Siege of Baler anniversary; (2) 10th Philippine-Spanish Friendship Day; (3) Bicentennial (200th anniversary) of the Cadiz Constitution of 1812
sub_topics: CJP's association with Senator Angara: met many decades ago when Angara was elected IBP President in 1979; joined him when Angara organized and became founding president of ALA in 1980; Angara as 'best trained and most well rounded potential President the Philippines will ever have'

UP Oblation connection: though not a UP alumnus, CJP treasures the Oblation because 'my classmates at Mapa High School and I used to go to the UP campus in the 1950s'; 15-centavo bus fare barrier to enrolling
The four virtues of Baler: 'bravery, honor, friendship, and progress, characterize every great nation and every great leader'

Historical timeline of the Siege: Filipino revolution 1896; Pact of Biak-na-Bato 1897; American navy and Dewey entered Manila Bay 1898; Filipino revolutionaries resumed; poor communications -- 50 Spanish soldiers in Baler didn't know of developments in Manila; Katipuneros of Baler launched uprising June 28, 1898; Capitan de las Morenas retreated to stone-walled Baler parish church; held 337 days despite deficiencies in supplies, food and occasional attacks

End of the Siege: June 2, 1899 -- only one officer and 30 soldiers came out alive; brought to Tarlac; 'treated with admiration for their bravery and dedication to their duty'; June 30, 1899: Aguinaldo decree directed that Cerezo and his men should be deemed 'not as prisoners but as friends'
Aguinaldo's decree: lauded 'the valor, constancy and heroism with which that handful of isolated men, without any hope of help, defended their banner for a period of one year'

Gallant fighters on both sides: 'the two sides fought the Baler war gallantly. Both the Filipinos and the Spaniards kept their battle lines to the best of their ability without treachery and without any ungentlemanly behavior'

Cadiz Constitution (March 19, 1812): enacted by the Spanish Cortes while on retreat from Napoleon's army; 303 representatives, 37 from overseas territories including the Philippines; Ventura de los Reyes of Vigan signed for the Philippines; limited monarchy; sovereignty vested in the people, not the king; universal male suffrage; freedom of the press; concept of private ownership of property; liberty of citizens and nationals of Spain

Philippine significance of Cadiz: first recognized Philippine representation in Spanish lawmaking; inspired the nationalist movement in the Philippines; many historians consider it 'our first sovereign charter'; followed by Biak na Bato (1897), Malolos (1898), 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions
Spain's legal legacy: Penal Code, Civil Code and Code of Commerce -- basic provisions still exist as good law today despite revisions
Three milestones summary: 113th Siege of Baler anniversary; 10th Philippine-Spanish Friendship Day; 200th Cadiz Constitution bicentennial

stances.claim: Baler's four virtues -- bravery in battle, honor in capitulation, friendship in victory, progress in peace -- are not just historical observations but an active model for international relations: 'these four virtues characterize every great nation and every great leader.' The Philippine-Spanish relationship today embodies this model as 'equal and sovereign partners in the world.'
stances.rhetorical_move: four-virtues-as-model: the Baler narrative as a template for ideal international conflict resolution and post-conflict friendship
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing historical lesson

stances.claim: The Cadiz Constitution of 1812 is the first Philippine Constitution in the historical sequence, predating the Biak-na-Bato, Malolos, 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions. This reframing of Philippine constitutional history as beginning with a Spanish document is a significant historical interpretation that most Filipinos overlook.
stances.rhetorical_move: Cadiz-as-first-Philippine-charter argument: extending Philippine constitutional history 86 years earlier than the Malolos Constitution by counting the Cadiz Constitution
stances.confidence: asserted as a historian's interpretation, not CJP's original claim (attributed to 'many historians')

notable_anecdotes: Aguinaldo's June 30, 1899 decree: after the Spanish cazadores surrendered, President Aguinaldo issued a presidential decree 'directing that Cerezo and his men should be deemed not as prisoners but as friends' and praised 'the valor, constancy and heroism with which that handful of isolated men, without any hope of help, defended their banner for a period of one year.' -- the most magnanimous gesture in Philippine-Spanish military history.

The 337 days: 50 Spanish cazadores in a stone-walled parish church, 'despite deficiencies in supplies, food and occasional attacks by the Katipuneros,' held for 337 days -- nearly a full year -- because poor communications left them unaware that the Spanish-American War had changed the geopolitical context.

Ventura de los Reyes of Vigan: among the 303 representatives at the Spanish Cortes that enacted the Cadiz Constitution, 37 were from overseas Spanish territories including the Philippines; 'the Cadiz Constitution was signed on behalf of the Philippines by Ventura de los Reyes of Vigan' -- the first Filipino representative in a European legislature.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered June 30, 2012 as the Guest of Honor address at the program marking the 113th Anniversary of the Historic Siege of Baler and the 10th Philippine-Spanish Friendship Day -- invited by Senator Edgardo J. Angara ('best trained and most well rounded potential President the Philippines will ever have'; IBP President 1979; ALA founding president 1980; longest serving senator) -- this address by CJP presents three milestones. The Siege of Baler: on June 28, 1898, Katipuneros launched an uprising; 50 Spanish cazadores under Capitan Enrique de las Morenas retreated to the stone-walled Baler parish church; unaware that the Spanish-American War had already changed the geopolitical context (poor communications), they held for 337 days before surrendering June 2, 1899 with only one officer and 30 soldiers alive; brought to Tarlac, they were 'treated with admiration for their bravery and dedication to their duty'; on June 30, 1899 -- exactly 113 years before this speech -- President Aguinaldo issued a presidential decree directing that Cerezo and his men be deemed 'not as prisoners but as friends,' praising 'the valor, constancy and heroism with which that handful of isolated men, without any hope of help, defended their banner for a period of one year.' CJP derives four virtues of Baler: 'bravery in battle; honor in capitulation; friendship in victory; and progress in peace -- these four virtues characterize every great nation and every great leader.' Second milestone: the 10th Philippine-Spanish Friendship Day, now a relationship of 'equal and sovereign partners in the world.' Third milestone: the bicentennial of the Cadiz Constitution (March 19, 1812) -- enacted while the Spanish Cortes was on retreat from Napoleon; 37 of its 303 representatives were from overseas territories; signed for the Philippines by Ventura de los Reyes of Vigan; established limited monarchy, popular sovereignty, universal male suffrage, freedom of the press and private property -- and, critically, recognized Philippine representation in Spanish lawmaking. CJP cites historians who consider it 'our first sovereign charter,' predating the Biak-na-Bato, Malolos, 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions. He also notes Spain's lasting legal legacy: the Penal Code, Civil Code and Code of Commerce.
